chapters.title: Chapter 5: Reducing Capital Gains Tax Legally

lessons.title: Reinvestment Exemptions: Buying a House or Capital Gains Bonds to Save Tax

body.text: The law will let a large long-term gain go untaxed if you put the money back into a house or into specified bonds within strict deadlines. These exemptions save lakhs, but every one of them has a clock, a cap and a lock-in.

children.text: Meena, a 51-year-old pharmacist in Nashik, sold an inherited plot for ₹60 lakh and made a long-term gain of ₹25 lakh. Her tax at 12.5% would be ₹3,12,500. She was already planning to buy a flat, and by routing the sale proceeds into it she cut that bill sharply. This lesson shows exactly how the three main reinvestment exemptions work and where people lose them.

body.caption: The main reinvestment exemptions under the Income-tax Act, 2025

body.title: Which Exemption Fits?
body.question: Ajay sells gold jewellery he has held for 10 years and makes a long-term gain. Which reinvestment exemption can he use?
options: Section 85, by buying capital gains bonds
Section 86, by buying a residential house with the sale proceeds
Section 82, by buying a residential house with the gain
None, because gold does not qualify for any exemption
body.explanation: Section 85 bonds only work for gains from land or buildings, so gold does not qualify. Section 82 requires the asset sold to be a residential house. Section 86 covers any long-term asset other than a residential house, including gold, shares and plots, if the net sale consideration goes into one residential house in India.

children.text: Section 86: Invest the Whole Sale Value, Not Just the Gain

markDefs.definition: Sale value minus transfer expenses, cost of acquisition and cost of improvement. Under section 82 only this amount needs to be reinvested; under section 86 the whole net consideration must be.

. For section 86 you must reinvest the whole net sale consideration to get a full exemption. Invest less and the exemption is scaled down proportionately.

body.title: Meena's Exemption
body.prompt: Meena's net sale consideration is ₹60,00,000, her long-term gain is ₹25,00,000 and she invests ₹45,00,000 in a new flat. What exemption can she claim under section 86, in rupees?
body.explanation: Exemption = ₹25,00,000 × ₹45,00,000 ÷ ₹60,00,000 = ₹18,75,000. Only ₹6,25,000 of her gain stays taxable, so her tax falls from ₹3,12,500 to ₹78,125. Had she invested the full ₹60,00,000, the entire gain would have been exempt.

body.text: Section 86 also has an ownership test. On the date of the sale you must not own more than one residential house other than the new one, and you cannot buy another house within 2 years or construct one within 3 years, apart from the new house. Break either condition and the exemption is withdrawn.

body.title: The Section 85 Limit
body.textWithBlank: Capital gains bonds under section 85 can only be used for long-term gains from the sale of ___ or building.
body.explanation: Section 85 (section 54EC of the 1961 Act) applies only to land or buildings. Gains from shares, gold, unlisted shares or mutual funds cannot be parked in these bonds.

stats.label: Investment window
stats.context: From the date of transfer of the land or building

stats.label: Maximum investment
stats.context: Per financial year, and capped across the two years covered by one six-month window

stats.label: Lock-in
stats.context: Bonds cannot be sold, transferred or used as loan security

stats.label: Interest
stats.context: Paid annually, taxed at your slab rate, with no TDS

children.text: Bonds are the simplest exemption to execute, but the money is stuck for five years at a modest rate. Ravi sells a shop and makes a ₹40 lakh long-term gain. Paying tax costs ₹5,00,000 at 12.5%, leaving ₹35,00,000 to invest elsewhere. Putting the full ₹40 lakh into bonds saves that tax but earns ₹2,10,000 a year before tax, or about ₹1,47,000 after tax at a 30% slab.

body.title: Ravi After 5 Years: Bonds vs Paying the Tax (Illustrative)

data.label: Pay tax, invest the rest at 7%

children.text: On these illustrative numbers, the bonds leave Ravi with about ₹47,35,000 after five years, against roughly ₹44,45,755 if he pays the tax and invests what is left at 7% before tax. The exemption wins here because the tax saved is large relative to the yield gap, but the gap narrows quickly if alternative returns are higher. Run your own numbers rather than assuming the exemption is always better.

body.text: The ₹50 lakh bond cap is per financial year and is also capped across the two financial years that a single six-month window can straddle. Selling in February and splitting ₹50 lakh in March and another ₹50 lakh in April does not double the exemption.

children.text: When the Money Is Not Spent Yet

events.title: The clock starts
events.description: All the time limits below run from the date the capital asset is transferred.

events.title: Section 85 bonds
events.description: Invest up to ₹50 lakh in specified bonds. Missing this window closes the option permanently.

events.title: Deposit unused money in a capital gains account
events.description: Money you have not yet spent on the new house must go into a Capital Gains Account Scheme account with a bank before you file, to keep the exemption alive.

events.title: Purchase of the new house
events.description: Or 1 year before the sale. Registration and payment records matter.

events.title: Construction of the new house
events.description: Applies where you build rather than buy, including most under-construction purchases.

events.title: Do not sell the new house
events.description: Selling the new house within 3 years withdraws the exemption and brings the earlier gain back to tax.

body.title: Sanjay Misses the Deposit
body.scenario: Sanjay sold a plot in August 2026 with a ₹35,00,000 long-term gain. He planned to buy a flat and claimed the section 86 exemption in his return, filed in July 2027. He had not bought anything yet, and the sale proceeds were still sitting in his savings account. He bought the flat in March 2028, well within two years.
body.modelAnswer: No. Money not yet spent on the new house has to be deposited in a Capital Gains Account Scheme account with a bank before the due date for filing the return. Sanjay left the proceeds in an ordinary savings account, so the unutilised amount fails the condition and the exemption on it can be denied, even though he bought the flat within two years. Had he deposited the money in a capital gains account before filing and then withdrawn it to pay the builder, the exemption would have held. This is one of the most common ways people lose a valid exemption.

body.title: Details Worth Knowing Before You Commit

children.text: The ₹10 crore cap: both section 82 and section 86 cap the cost of the new house that qualifies at ₹10 crore. Gains beyond that are taxed normally.
Two houses, once in a lifetime: under section 82, if the capital gain does not exceed ₹2 crore, you can buy or construct two houses instead of one. This choice can be used only once.
Capital gains account: withdrawals must be used for the house within the time limits. Any balance left unused at the end of the period becomes taxable in that later year.

Selling the new house early: if you sell the new house within 3 years, the exemption is withdrawn. For section 85 bonds, selling, transferring or taking a loan against them within 5 years does the same.

Joint ownership and home loans: the exemption follows the person whose gain it is and who invests. Adding a spouse as joint owner, or funding part of the purchase with a loan, needs care in documentation.

body.label: What Meena Saved
body.context: By routing ₹45,00,000 of her ₹60,00,000 sale proceeds into a flat, her tax fell from ₹3,12,500 to ₹78,125. Investing the entire ₹60,00,000 would have removed the remaining tax altogether.

body.title: If You Are Planning a Big Asset Sale
steps: Work out the expected long-term gain and the tax before you agree a sale date
Decide which exemption fits the asset you are selling: house, other asset, or land and building
For bonds, diarise the six-month deadline from the date of transfer and the ₹50 lakh cap
For a house, keep sale proceeds identifiable and plan the purchase or construction timeline
Open a Capital Gains Account Scheme account before your ITR due date for any unspent amount
Keep the new house for at least 3 years, and bonds for 5 years, to avoid the exemption being withdrawn

points: Section 82 lets you reinvest a house sale gain into another house; only the gain needs reinvesting
Section 86 covers gains from other assets but requires the whole net sale consideration to go into one house
Section 85 allows land or building gains to go into specified bonds within 6 months, capped at ₹50 lakh with a 5-year lock-in
Unspent sale proceeds must be deposited in a Capital Gains Account Scheme account before the ITR due date
Both house exemptions are capped at a ₹10 crore cost for the new house
Selling the new house within 3 years, or the bonds within 5 years, withdraws the exemption

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or investment advice. Amounts, bond rates and alternative returns are illustrative. Sections reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 for tax year 2026-27, with 1961 Act sections in brackets. Reinvestment exemptions are fact-specific and frequently litigated, so consult a qualified tax professional before relying on one.
